newsitem.title: USA: Possible nuke shutdown worries Maine officials.
newsitem.headline: Possible nuke shutdown worries Maine officials.

text.p: Maine officials Wednesday said they will examine the economic impact of a shutdown of Maine Yankee although they still hope a buyer will be found for the troubled nuclear plant.
Maine Yankee's owners announced Tuesday they will suspend efforts to restart the 25-year-old plant in Wiscasset while they decide if it can be sold or should be permanently closed.

The "preservation" plan will reduce planned spending on the 910-megawatt plant in 1997 by $41 million, forcing the elimination in the next few days of 900 contract workers and likely layoff of 50 permanent employees in the next few weeks.

Maine Gov. Angus King said he will appoint a task force to study the economic impact of a plant shut down on both the state and Wiscasset - where the facility pays for 90 percent of the town and school budgets
"This raises an awful lot of questions...this is uncharted territory," King told reporters. The plant was licensed to run until 2008, although it has been off-line for much of the past three years.

Maine Yankee's board said it will continue to search for a buyer until early fall, but officials acknowledge they are not optimistic that the facility - which has been plagued by safety problems - can be sold.
The nuclear plant has not operated at full capacity since 1995. Its latest shutdown began Dec 6, 1996 after officials discovered misrouted electrical cables.

Among the issues state officials said must be addressed is how to pay for decommissioning. Plant officials estimate that it will cost $369 million to decommission the facility but the fund to pay for it only has $169 million.

Maine Yankee is 38 percent owned by Central Maine Power Co, 20 percent each by New England Electric System and Northeast Utilities, seven percent by Bangor Hydro-Electric Co, five percent by Maine Public Service Co, and 10 percent by other New England utilities.
